# Whatever Comes to Me

There's a particular kind of silence that happens at three in the morning, the kind where you can hear the hum of the refrigerator like it's telling you secrets. I'm thinking about that now, about how we rarely sit with silence anymore, how we've engineered it out of our lives with notifications and podcasts and the constant murmur of background television. But silence is still here, waiting, patient as a cat that knows you'll eventually come home.

I've been thinking a lot lately about the things we lose by moving too quickly. Not the big dramatic things—not opportunities or relationships, though those matter—but the small observations that require you to actually stop. The way light falls through a window at a specific angle for maybe forty-five minutes before it shifts forever. The expression on someone's face when they're thinking about something they don't want to say. The exact texture of air on the day the season changes, that moment when autumn arrives and it's so sudden you almost miss it, and then it's too late, it's here, summer is dead.

I read something recently about how our ancestors could name dozens of different snows, how the Inuit language supposedly had all these words for different types of snow depending on whether it was falling or had already accumulated or was being blown by wind. I don't know if that's actually true—I think linguists say it probably isn't, that it's one of those facts that feels true so we just keep repeating it—but I like the idea anyway. I like the idea that you can know something so well that you need multiple words for it. That intimate knowledge of a single thing. That's what I wish for, mostly. One deep thing instead of a thousand shallow ones.

The coffee shop near my apartment has a woman who comes in every Tuesday morning. She orders an Americano and sits in the corner booth and reads physical books—actual paper books with broken spines. Last week she was reading something with a blue cover that I couldn't quite see the title of, and I found myself wondering what was happening in her story, whether it was good, whether she was the kind of person who reads the ending first or the kind who reads every word in order. I will probably never know anything about this woman, and yet she's become somehow important to me, a small anchor in the chaos of the week. Proof that people still do things slowly.

I think a lot about what we're going to miss about this time. Someday—maybe someday soon—we'll look back and think about what we were doing right now, in this specific moment, and we won't quite believe we didn't treasure it more. Or we won't be able to remember it clearly enough to regret not treasuring it. It'll just be gone, absorbed into the general wash of days. This thought makes me sad and also, strangely, peaceful. It means nothing is wasted because it's all temporary anyway. Your worst day, your most boring Tuesday, that time you were stuck in traffic for two hours and didn't accomplish anything—it all matters because it all ends.

There's something beautiful in that, if you can stop fighting it long enough to see it.

I've been thinking about the word "home" a lot. About what makes a place feel like home and whether it has to be a place at all, or whether it could be a person or a song or that specific coffee shop corner where the woman with the blue book sits. I've lived in the same apartment for three years and I still don't feel like I'm home there, and I wonder if I'm too old to learn, or if home isn't something you arrive at but something you build so slowly you don't notice until one day you're sitting somewhere and you realize you're not checking the time, not thinking about leaving, just... existing.

I watched a video recently of an old man playing piano. He was probably in his eighties, playing something classical that I couldn't name, and his hands had arthritis but they still remembered all the notes. And I thought about what it means to know something that well, to have your body remember something your mind might struggle to consciously recall. That's the kind of knowledge I want—not in my head, but in my bones.

The weather's been strange lately. Too warm, then too cold, then warm again. The trees don't know what to do. There's this one tree right outside my window that's been half-green and half-yellow for two weeks now, like it can't decide what season it's supposed to be in. I relate to that tree.

I think we're all the tree, actually. Half of us is ready for something new and half of us wants to hold onto what we know. Half of us wants connection and half of us wants to be alone with our thoughts and a book with a broken spine. There's no resolving that contradiction. We just live in it.

Okay, here's what I know: the refrigerator is still humming. Somewhere, the woman is probably sleeping, and she'll wake up next Tuesday and go back to the coffee shop and order an Americano and sit in the corner booth and continue her story. Seasons will change. The tree will figure it out eventually. And we'll all keep moving forward through our days, mostly distracted, occasionally stopping long enough to notice something beautiful or strange or sad, and then we'll forget it again, and then maybe someone will remember it for us.

That's enough, I think. That has to be enough.

The silence at three in the morning is still here, and I'm going to sit with it a little longer, because I can, because I have nowhere to be tomorrow that can't wait. The refrigerator hums its secret. The tree outside is neither one thing nor another, and that's okay. Everything is temporary and that's the best news I've heard all week.
